content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is a blood product that contains procoagulant factors and is sometimes used during cardiovascular surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding. This review aimed to evaluate whether the use of FFP in cardiovascular surgery affects mortality risk. The objective of this review was to assess the risk-to-benefit ratio of FFP transfusion in cardiovascular surgery, either for treating bleeding or as a preventive measure against bleeding. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search across 11 bibliographic databases and four ongoing trial registries, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), and the ISRCTN Register. The search was completed on April 21, 2015, and included studies without restrictions on language or publication status. References from identified trials and relevant review articles were also examined. The review included randomized controlled trials involving patients undergoing major cardiac or vascular surgery. Participants were assigned to either an FFP group or a comparator group (no plasma, clinical plasma of any type, or plasma-derived blood products). The review included patients of all ages, including neonates, children, and adults. Studies involving plasmapheresis or plasma exchange were excluded. Two authors independently screened all citations and abstracts identified through the search strategy. They also assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted data independently. The authors carefully noted whether FFP was used therapeutically or prophylactically in each trial. A total of 15 trials, involving 755 participants, were included in the review. Fourteen trials evaluated the prophylactic use of FFP compared to no FFP, while one trial compared the therapeutic use of two types of plasma. The timing of FFP administration varied across studies, including transfusion during heparin neutralization and cessation of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) (seven trials), as part of CPB priming (four trials), after induction of anesthesia (one trial), and postoperatively (two trials). Twelve trials excluded patients undergoing emergency surgery, and nine excluded patients with coagulopathies. The trials were generally small, with only four reporting a pre-specified sample size calculation. None of the trials were adequately powered to detect changes in mortality as a primary outcome. Most of the included studies had a high or unclear risk of bias. There was no difference in mortality between the intervention and control groups in the six trials (287 patients) that reported this outcome. The evidence for this finding was of very low quality. Similarly, there was no significant difference in blood loss within the first 24 hours for neonatal or pediatric patients (four trials, 138 patients; low-quality evidence) or adult patients (one trial, 120 patients). The mean difference in blood loss for neonates and children was -1.46 mL/kg (95% confidence interval [CI]: -4.7 to 1.78 mL/kg), and for adults, it was -12.00 mL (95% CI: -101.16 to 77.16 mL). FFP transfusion was found to be inferior to the control group in preventing the need for red blood cell transfusion. The Peto odds ratio (OR) for this outcome was 2.57 (95% CI: 1.30 to 5.08; moderate-quality evidence). However, there was a significant reduction in prothrombin time within two hours of FFP transfusion in eight trials (210 patients; moderate-quality evidence), with a mean difference of -0.71 seconds (95% CI: -1.28 to -0.13 seconds). There was no difference in the risk of returning to the operating room for reoperation between the FFP and control groups (eight trials, 398 patients; moderate-quality evidence). The Peto OR for this outcome was 0.81 (95% CI: 0.26 to 2.57). Only one study reported adverse events as an outcome, and it found no significant adverse events associated with FFP transfusion. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the prophylactic use of FFP in patients without coagulopathy undergoing elective cardiac surgery. There was insufficient evidence to evaluate the use of FFP in patients with coagulopathies or those undergoing emergency surgery. Although no adverse events were reported with FFP transfusion, there was a significant increase in the number of patients requiring red blood cell transfusion in the FFP group. Variability in outcome reporting across trials prevented meta-analysis for many outcomes, and most studies had a high risk of bias. The authors emphasized the need for further well-powered studies to evaluate the safety and efficacy of FFP or comparable pro-hemostatic agents. Specifically, future research should determine whether reductions in prothrombin time translate into meaningful clinical benefits. Overall, the evidence from randomized controlled trials is insufficient to support the prophylactic use of FFP in cardiac surgery.
